SK1060 Use an index-from-end expression

An element access whose index counts back from the collection's own Count or Length is an index-from-end expression.

CategoryModernization
Default severitysuggestion
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, safe
Language version floorC# 8.0
Since1.3
ReSharperUseIndexFromEndExpression (resharper_use_index_from_end_expression_highlighting)

Why

items[items.Count - 1] names the collection twice and subtracts, and the reader has to check that both names are the same collection before believing the expression means "the last one". items[^1] says it, names the receiver once, and cannot be written with the wrong collection on one side — the copy-paste defect this shape produces is exactly a[b.Count - 1], which compiles and is wrong. The subtraction is also the arithmetic the compiler was going to emit anyway: ^1 lowers to Count - 1, so the rewrite costs nothing and removes the only place a person can get it wrong.

Example

Instead of:

var last = items[items.Count - 1];
var previous = buffer[buffer.Length - offset];

Write:

var last = items[^1];
var previous = buffer[^offset];

When it does not fire

⚠ `^` is not available on everything that has a `Count`. The language's implicit index support needs a countable type and an int indexer, and IEnumerable<T> has neither — so the rule reads the indexed type rather than the shape of the expression, and admits only an array, a string, a type with a real System.Index indexer (Span<T>, ReadOnlySpan<T>), or a type implementing IList<T>/IReadOnlyList<T>. ⚠ `Dictionary<int, V>` is countable and has an `int` indexer, so `d[^1]` compiles and means the entry keyed Count - 1 — the same program, spelled as if it were the last element. The IList<T> restriction is what keeps that out, and it is the reason the rule is not simply "the type is countable". ⚠ The receiver of the element access and the receiver of .Count/.Length must be the same chain of plain names, so a[b.Count - 1] is never rewritten and nothing that could have a side effect is evaluated a different number of times. ⚠ The subtrahend is admitted only as a positive integer literal or a plain `int`-typed name path. ^0 is Count, which throws where Count - 0 also throws but is a different sentence, and a negative constant reaches Index's constructor, which throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException where the subtraction would have thrown IndexOutOfRangeException. ⚠ Silent below C# 8, silent inside an expression tree where the indexer pattern is not expressible, and silent where System.Index is not accessible — which is not the same question as whether it exists. System.Memory ships an internal System.Index for netstandard2.0, so a presence check alone reported sixteen findings on Skala's own netstandard2.0 projects, every one of whose fixes failed to compile with CS0518. The gate is the compiler's own accessibility test. The rule is one shape with one floor, so the gate is per-rule.
